title: The Kindly Hymn
premise: Elodie Vasquez, a pest controller with a habit of counting doors and keeping lights on, is called to the village of Hollowmere to deal with something that leaves fingerprints on the inside of sealed windows. When the church bell — melted down in 1911 — rings at midnight, Elodie learns the village's founding families invited something in generations ago, and it has been fed ever since. As the harvest moon rises, he must survive until sunrise while uncovering who among the villagers still tends the invitation, discovering that his own grandmother was one of them and that her inheritance now marks him as the next keeper. In the end, Elodie refuses the inheritance, breaks the bell's silence by ringing it himself, and walks out at dawn as Hollowmere's doors finally stay shut behind him.
about_author: Elodie Iversen grew up in a coastal fishing town where every house had a story about the water, and she never stopped writing down what people were afraid of. She lives in rural Norfolk with too many locks on her doors, all of which she counts nightly.

chapters.title: Fingerprints
chapters.summary: POV: Elodie. A routine call about rats in an empty cottage ends with Elodie finding small handprints on the inside of painted-shut windows, dusted in flour from a kitchen no one uses. He keeps the lights on and counts eleven doors on his way out. Emotional beat: unease disguised as professionalism.

chapters.title: The Kindly Hymn
chapters.summary: POV: Elodie. The village of Hollowmere hires him for a recurring 'infestation' — third contractor this year. At the pub, old men hum a hymn no one will name, and the landlady warns him not to work past dark. Emotional beat: the sense of being welcomed into something wrong.

chapters.title: Eleven Doors
chapters.summary: POV: Elodie. Surveying the manor where the activity centers, Elodie counts doors out of habit and gets twelve twice, eleven once, though nothing moves. He finds claw-grooves beside every doorframe, worn smooth by decades of touching. Emotional beat: dread settling into method.

chapters.title: The Bell That Isn't
chapters.summary: POV: Elodie. At midnight the church bell rings — but parish records show it was melted for scrap in 1911. Villagers light candles and do not look outside. Elodie, alone in his van, feels the sound pass through him like a summons. Emotional beat: the moment the ordinary world tears.

chapters.title: What Was Invited
chapters.summary: POV: Elodie. The vicar, Reverend Ashe, half-drunk, tells him the village 'keeps an arrangement' — something was invited before the harvest moon generations ago and must be tended or it takes freely. He begs Elodie to leave before moonrise. Emotional beat: pity tangled with complicity.

chapters.title: The Keeper's Ledger
chapters.summary: POV: Elodie. In the manor archive Elodie finds a ledger of names — keepers who fed the thing each harvest, entries ending 1911, the year of the bell. The last name is Vasquez. His grandmother's maiden name. Emotional beat: inheritance as infection.

chapters.title: Doors That Count Back
chapters.summary: POV: Elodie. Night two: the manor's doors begin opening and closing in sequence, walking him deeper into the house. Fingerprints now appear at his own eye level, fresh, still wet. He realizes it has been studying him since the cottage. Emotional beat: hunted inside a labyrinth.

chapters.title: The Harvest Moon Rises
chapters.summary: POV: Elodie. Moonrise comes early and orange. The village goes silent mid-hymn. Every door in Hollowmere unlocks at once, and Elodie understands the deadline: hold out until sunrise, or become the next keeper by default. Emotional beat: the trap closing.

chapters.title: Neighbors
chapters.summary: POV: Elodie. Villagers appear at the manor gates carrying lanterns, smiling, asking him to 'come home.' Their kindness is the horror — they genuinely want to spare him pain by making him willing. Emotional beat: belonging offered as a knife.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Room
chapters.summary: POV: Elodie. He finds a sealed room preserved since 1911: his grandmother's childhood things, a cot, chalk tallies on the wall counting harvests survived. A letter begins 'If you are reading this, you have my hands.' Emotional beat: grief meeting inheritance.

chapters.title: The Letter
chapters.summary: POV: Elodie. The letter explains the arrangement: the keeper feeds it willingly and it spares the village; refuse, and it hunts until someone says yes. His grandmother fled rather than serve, and the debt passed down the blood. Emotional beat: fury at the dead and the living alike.

chapters.title: Wet Handprints
chapters.summary: POV: Elodie. The thing manifests fully for the first time — a shape made of doorways and reaching hands, its touch leaving prints that match Elodie's own. It is patient, almost tender. It only wants to be let in properly. Emotional beat: intimacy as threat.

chapters.title: Ashe's Bargain
chapters.summary: POV: Elodie. Reverend Ashe offers to take Elodie's place if Elodie opens the door for him — the invitation needs a Vasquez's consent. Elodie sees the vicar's terror and temptation warring. He refuses. Emotional beat: power corrupting even the sympathetic.

chapters.title: Counting to Sunrise
chapters.summary: POV: Elodie. Hours before dawn. Elodie barricades with furniture, keeps lights burning, counts doors aloud to stay sane. The house rearranges; the count changes; his voice starts answering itself from other rooms. Emotional beat: endurance fraying.

chapters.title: The Twelfth Door
chapters.summary: POV: Elodie. A twelfth door appears where there were always eleven — old, scarred, warm to the touch. Behind it, his grandmother's voice, young again, asking him to open up like she never could bring herself to. Emotional beat: love weaponized.

chapters.title: What the Bell Remembers
chapters.summary: POV: Elodie. In the crypt beneath the church, Elodie finds the bell wasn't melted — it was buried, silenced because its ring binds the thing to the terms of the invitation. The 1911 keepers cheated it, and it has been collecting ever since. Emotional beat: revelation as leverage.

chapters.title: Terms of Surrender
chapters.summary: POV: Elodie. Sunrise nears. The thing offers everything: belonging, safety, the village's love, his grandmother back. Elodie nearly says yes — the loneliness of his whole life rising to meet the offer. Emotional beat: the corruption of comfort.

chapters.title: Refusal
chapters.summary: POV: Elodie. At the threshold, hand on the twelfth door, Elodie speaks his refusal — not bravely, but honestly, admitting he'd wanted to belong and choosing himself anyway. The house screams through every doorframe. Emotional beat: costly self-acceptance.

chapters.title: Ringing It Himself
chapters.summary: POV: Elodie. He digs out the buried bell and rings it with a sledgehammer as the sky pales. The true peal rebinds the terms: the invitation expires with the last Vasquez keeper — him. The thing unravels through the village, door by counted door. Emotional beat: catharsis through noise.

chapters.title: Sunrise
chapters.summary: POV: Elodie. Dawn. The villagers wake with no memory of their arrangement, weeping without knowing why. Ashe remembers everything and cannot meet his eyes. Elodie packs his van amid candle stubs and cold lanterns. Emotional beat: hollow, hard-won relief.

chapters.title: The Last Count
chapters.summary: POV: Elodie. Driving out, Elodie counts doors one final time out of habit — and stops himself, letting the number go uncounted. In the mirror, Hollowmere shrinks, its church tower bare and silent. Emotional beat: breaking the inheritance by letting go of the ritual.

chapters.title: Hands Like Mine
chapters.summary: POV: Elodie. Weeks later, a new call comes from another village with a melted bell. Elodie looks at his own hands — his grandmother's hands — and takes the job anyway, determined to end every arrangement the ledgers record. Emotional beat: chosen purpose over inherited curse.
